22 A copper wire has length 1.7 m and uniform diameter 0.64 mm.
The Young modulus of copper is 1.2  1011
Pa.
What is the spring constant of the wire?
A
2.3  104
N m–1
B
9.1  104
N m–1
C
4.5  107
N m–1
D
7.1  107
N m–1

hints: Notice the wire length $1.7 \text{ m}$, diameter $0.64 \text{ mm}$ and Young modulus $1.2 \times 10^{11} \text{ Pa}$ - first convert diameter to radius in metres.
Recall Young modulus $E = (F/A)/(x/L)$ and spring constant $k = F/x$, so combine them to get $k = EA/L$.
Calculate $A = \pi r^2$ with $r = 0.32 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$, then multiply by $E$ and divide by $L = 1.7 \text{ m}$ and check the power of ten.
walkthrough: Identify the data: $L = 1.7 \text{ m}$, $d = 0.64 \text{ mm} = 0.64 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$, so $r = 0.32 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$, and $E = 1.2 \times 10^{11} \text{ Pa}$.
State the governing relations: $E = stress/strain = (F/A)/(x/L)$ and $k = F/x$. Rearranging gives $k = EA/L$.
Calculate the cross-sectional area: $A = \pi r^2 = \pi \times (0.32 \times 10^{-3})^2 \approx 3.22 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}^2$.
Complete the division: $k \approx 2.3 \times 10^4 \text{ N m}^{-1}$ with correct units of force per extension. This is option A.

A.explanation: Correct. $k = EA/L$ with $A = 3.2 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}^2$ gives about $2.3 \times 10^4 \text{ N m}^{-1}$.

B.explanation: Too large by factor 4. This results from using the 0.64 mm diameter as the radius when calculating $A = \pi r^2$.

C.explanation: Far too large. This comes from mishandling the $\text{mm}$ to $\text{m}$ conversion and the area calculation for the 0.64 mm diameter.

D.explanation: Far too large. This comes from incorrect cross-sectional area combined with length and unit errors in $k = EA/L$.
